B1.title: Book One: God
B1.bookSummary: Book One of the Summa Contra Gentiles undertakes to demonstrate truths about God that are attainable by human reason alone, without reliance upon divine revelation. This approach reflects Aquinas's conviction that since non-believers do not accept scriptural authority, the refutation of errors and the establishment of divine truth must proceed through philosophical argumentation accessible to reason. The book systematically establishes God's existence through the classical five ways (the argument from motion, from efficient causation, from possibility and necessity, from degrees of perfection, and from the order of the universe). It then demonstrates God's essential attributes: God's simplicity (freedom from composition), God's perfection and infinity, God's unchangeableness, God's eternality, God's unity, and God's incorporeality and immateriality. Throughout, Aquinas shows how God must be understood as pure actuality (actus purus) without potentiality, and as the ultimate source and ground of all being.

B2.title: Book Two: Creation
B2.bookSummary: Book Two examines God's creative activity and the nature of creation. Aquinas establishes that creation—the production of beings from non-being—manifests God's power and is not contrary to reason. The book analyzes what it means for God to create and sustains that creation is a free act of God's will, not a necessary emanation. It then investigates the nature of creatures themselves: how all creatures possess being participated from God (who alone is Being subsisting), how creatures are constituted of essence and existence, how they possess reality and goodness even as dependent beings. The work treats extensively the different orders of creation: the nature of angels (spiritual creatures), the material universe including the celestial bodies, and finally human beings as composites of body and soul. Special attention is given to human nature: the rational soul as the substantial form of the body, the intellect's capacity to know all things, and the will's orientation toward good. The book also addresses the freedom of human choice and how divine foreknowledge is compatible with human freedom.

B3.title: Book Three: Providence and Divine Governance
B3.bookSummary: Book Three treats God's providential governance of creation and the principles of human conduct and virtue. Having established what God is and what God creates, Aquinas now addresses how all things are directed toward God as their ultimate end. Divine providence is shown to be necessary: God must govern and direct all creatures toward their proper ends, and this governance is exercised through particular providence concerning individual creatures and acts. The work then systematically expounds the virtues as the means by which humans achieve their ultimate end (beatitude, or union with God). It covers the cardinal virtues (prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice) and theological virtues (faith, hope, and charity), explaining how these virtues perfect human faculties and direct human conduct toward the good. A substantial portion addresses the natural law—the divine reason governing all creatures, apprehended by humans through reason—and the eternal law as the source of all particular laws. The book also treats vice and sin as departures from the natural law and divine governance, and explains how grace perfects and elevates nature toward the supernatural end.

B4.title: Book Four: Salvation and Christ
B4.bookSummary: Book Four addresses God's plan for human salvation through Christ and the sacraments, completing the arc of Aquinas's philosophical theology. Having demonstrated through reason alone what can be known of God, creation, and divine governance, Aquinas now addresses truths that exceed reason and depend upon Christian revelation: the mystery of the Incarnation and the redemptive work of Christ. The book establishes that the Incarnation—God's assumption of human nature in the person of the divine Word—is fitting and necessary for human salvation. It demonstrates how Christ, as both God and man, is the perfect mediator between God and humanity, whose passion and death accomplish the redemption of mankind. Christ's sacrifice is shown to have infinite value because offered by a divine person, and thus capable of satisfying for the sins of all. The work then addresses the principal means by which Christ's redemptive grace is communicated to believers: the sacraments, especially Baptism (the gateway to salvation) and the Eucharist (the perpetuation of Christ's sacrifice and nourishment of the faithful). Special attention is given to the Incarnate Word's wisdom and power, and how Christ serves as the exemplar and principal cause of grace in the Church.
